steps.prompt: $10! = 3{,}628{,}800$ ends in two zeros. Where do those zeros come from? How many zeros do you think $100!$ ends in?
steps.placeholder: The zeros come from… my guess is…

cards.title: Zeros come from tens
cards.body: Each zero at the end is a factor $10 = 2 \times 5$. A factorial has far more $2$s than $5$s, so count the $5$s: multiples of $5$ give one each, multiples of $25$ give one more, multiples of $125$ one more again. Zeros of $n!$ $= \left\lfloor \frac{n}{5} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \frac{n}{25} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \frac{n}{125} \right\rfloor + \cdots$

cards.title: Worked example: zeros of 100!
cards.problem: How many zeros does $100!$ end with?

steps.text: There are $20$ multiples of $5$ up to $100$.

try.prompt: How many multiples of $5$ are there from $1$ to $100$?

steps.text: $25, 50, 75, 100$ each have a second $5$: that adds $4$.

try.prompt: How many multiples of $25$ are there from $1$ to $100$?
How many zeros does $100!$ end with?

cards.title: Any prime in a factorial
cards.body: The same count works for any prime $p$: the power of $p$ in $n!$ is $\left\lfloor \frac{n}{p} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p^2} \right\rfloor + \left\lfloor \frac{n}{p^3} \right\rfloor + \cdots$ For $6^k$ or $12^k$, find the power of each prime and see which one runs out first.

cards.title: Worked example: twos in 10!
cards.problem: What is the largest $k$ such that $2^k$ divides $10!$?

steps.text: Multiples of $2$: $5$. Multiples of $4$: $2$. Multiples of $8$: $1$.

try.prompt: How many multiples of $4$ are there from $1$ to $10$?

cards.title: The common trap: counting 25 only once
cards.body: $25 = 5 \times 5$ gives TWO fives, and $125$ gives three. Stopping at $\left\lfloor \frac{n}{5} \right\rfloor$ undercounts. Also, $n!$ never ends in exactly $5$ zeros: going from $24!$ to $25!$ jumps from $4$ zeros to $6$.

prompts: Why do we count $5$s and not $2$s for the zeros at the end of $n!$?
